## 1. Load the processed data

```{r load}
# Load psych package
library(psych)

h1Data <- read.csv("data/processed_data/h1_revised.csv")
h2Data <- read.csv("data/processed_data/h2_revised.csv")

```

## 2. Look at "distribution" of the count variable (Employment Status) 
```{r histogram}
#H1
## Count Bargraph for Employment (categorical variable)

library(ggplot2)

Employ_bar <- ggplot(data = h1Data,
                     aes(x = Employment_group,
                     fill = Employment_group)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(x="Employment Status",
       y="Amount of People",
       fill="Employment_group")
Employ_bar
```

## 3 Look at distributions (using Histogram)

```{r histogram}

# histogram groups num. values into intervals (bins).
# Bar height shows how many observations fall in each interval.
# Start by looking at the distribution before calculating summary statistics.

#H1 variable
hist(h1Data$ind_rev_mean)
## Add readable labels to the same histogram.
hist(h1Data$ind_rev_mean,
     main = "Distribution of Individualistic Attitudes",
     xlab = "Individualistic Attitudes (1-7)")

## Change bin width (because scores have been averaged and this portrays it on the scale of the original measurement)
hist(h1Data$ind_rev_mean,
     breaks = seq(from = 0, to = 7, by=1),
     main = "Distribution of Individualistic Attitudes",
     xlab = "Individualistic Attitudes (1-7)")
#Output:normally distributed

#H2 variables
hist(h2Data$Gender_Equality_mean)
#output:left skewed

hist(h2Data$appearance_time_sum)
#output:right skewed
```

## One statistic at a time for ind_rev_mean variable 
```{r individual stats}

#H1: Employment Status 
# Table: count how many people are in each category.
table(h1Data$Employment_group, useNA = "ifany")

#H1: Individualistic attitudes

## measures of central tendency
mean(h1Data$ind_rev_mean, na.rm = TRUE)
median(h1Data$ind_rev_mean, na.rm = TRUE)

##measures of variability
# Range: return the minimum and maximum.
range(h1Data$ind_rev_mean, na.rm = TRUE)
# IQR: the 75th percentile minus the 25th percentile.
IQR(h1Data$ind_rev_mean, na.rm = TRUE)

```

## Several statistics at once for all variables
```{r descriptive stats}
summary(h1Data$ind_rev_mean)
psych::describe(h1Data$ind_rev_mean)

summary(h2Data$Gender_Equality_mean)
psych::describe(h2Data$Gender_Equality_mean)

summary(h2Data$appearance_time_sum)
psych::describe(h2Data$appearance_time_sum)
```

##Standardizing variables
```{r standardizing variables}
# scale() uses z = ((original score - mean) / (standard deviation)) by default.
# Keep the original commitment scores and store the standardized values separately.
# scale() returns a matrix; as.numeric() makes a simple numeric column (this way its easily added to the dataframe).

#Standardize H1:Individualistic Attitudes
h1Data$ind_att_z <- as.numeric(scale(h1Data$ind_rev_mean))
head(h1Data[, c("ind_rev_mean", "ind_att_z")])

#Standardize H2: Gender Equality Attitudes
h2Data$gender_equality_z <- as.numeric(scale(h2Data$Gender_Equality_mean))

#Standardize H2: Time Spent on Appearance
h2Data$appearance_time_z <- as.numeric(scale(h2Data$appearance_time_sum))
```

##Covariance and Correlation for H2
```{r}
# Covariance describes whether two variables tend to move together.
## Positive: higher values tend to occur together. Negative: higher values tend to accompany lower values.
## Its size depends on the units and is not restricted to -1 through 1.

# Pearson correlation expresses a linear association on a -1 to 1 scale.

#Covariance for H2 
cov(h2Data$Gender_Equality_mean, h2Data$appearance_time_sum, use = "complete.obs")

# Correlation for H2
cor(h2Data$Gender_Equality_mean, h2Data$appearance_time_sum, use = "complete.obs")
## output: small negative correlation coefficient 

#Correlation Matrix for H2
## Select numerical variables only; do not include participant IDs or category codes.
corData <- h2Data[, c("Gender_Equality_mean", "appearance_time_sum")]
## A correlation matrix gives the correlation for each pair of columns.
### The diagonal is 1 because each variable is correlated with itself.
cor(corData, use = "complete.obs")
```


### H1: Descriptive stats for Individualistic Attitudes by Employment Group

```{Descriptive stats for individualistic Attitudes by  Employment Variable Category H1}
# aggregate() allows to calculate statistics seperately for different groups in the dataset
## ind_rev_mean ~ Employment_group tells R to calculate the statistic seperately for each Employment_group

#mean
aggregate(ind_rev_mean ~ Employment_group,
          data = h1Data,
          FUN = mean,
          na.rm = TRUE)
#median
aggregate(ind_rev_mean ~ Employment_group,
          data = h1Data,
          FUN = median,
          na.rm = TRUE)
#standard deviation
aggregate(ind_rev_mean ~ Employment_group,
          data = h1Data,
          FUN = sd,
          na.rm = TRUE)

```
